items.auditTesting: The auditor samples five suppliers across tiers and confirms each has a current assessment, that the tier reflects the data and connectivity involved, and that identified findings were remediated within the agreed period. The auditor traces a supplier access review and checks that entitlements for suppliers are reconciled and removed when the contract ends. A finding is raised where a supplier holding sensitive data has no current assessment, where the assessment is a self-declared questionnaire with no supporting evidence, or where supplier access persists after contract expiry.
commonGaps: Security questionnaires sent once at onboarding and never refreshed
Tiering based on spend rather than on data sensitivity and connectivity
Subcontractors and cloud sub-processors not covered by the assessment
Findings recorded but with no remediation deadline, owner or tracking
interviewQuestions: How is a supplier tier assigned and who signs it off?
What do you do when a critical supplier refuses to provide assessment evidence?
How do you confirm supplier access is removed at the end of a contract?
items.scenario: A retail group found that one of its biggest logistics suppliers had quietly subcontracted parcel scanning to a regional operator whose security posture was never assessed. The new tiering model required suppliers to disclose their own processing chain, and the logistics supplier's contract was amended so that any new sub-processor required prior approval and evidence. The group also used the incident to justify pulling its reconciliation and claims processing out of the supplier's estate entirely, reducing the exposure rather than only monitoring it.

items.title: Addressing information security within supplier agreements
items.objective: Defines information security requirements that must be included in supplier agreements so that external parties are contractually bound to protect information and support the organisation’s security objectives.
items.whyItExists: Supplier relationships create dependencies that operational controls alone cannot govern. Without explicit contractual requirements, expectations for confidentiality, incident notification, audit rights, subcontracting and service continuity remain informal and difficult to enforce when a dispute or incident occurs.
items.riskAddressed: Supplier services that process or affect information without enforceable security obligations, increasing the likelihood of misuse, delayed incident reporting or inadequate assurance.
items.implementationGuidance: Identify security requirements based on supplier tier, data sensitivity, connectivity and regulatory obligations, then translate them into standard contract clauses and schedules. Cover confidentiality, acceptable use, access control, encryption, logging, vulnerability and patch expectations where relevant, incident notification timelines, right to audit or obtain assurance, subcontractor approval, data return and secure deletion at exit, and consequences for non-compliance. Align legal, procurement and security review so clauses are negotiated before signature, track approved deviations with compensating controls, and maintain evidence that executed agreements contain the required terms for in-scope suppliers.
evidenceExamples: Executed supplier agreement with information security schedule
Standard security clause library approved by legal
Deviation register for negotiated exceptions
Supplier assurance package linked to contract
items.auditTesting: Sample in-scope supplier contracts and verify required security clauses are present, appropriate to the service and consistent with the risk assessment. Confirm deviations were approved, compensating controls recorded and incident notification or audit provisions are practical to exercise.
commonGaps: Generic confidentiality clauses used instead of service-specific security requirements
No right to audit or obtain independent assurance
Exit, data return and deletion obligations missing
Security terms negotiated after contract signature
interviewQuestions: Show me the security requirements included in a recent high-risk supplier contract.
How do you ensure incident notification timelines are enforceable?
What happens when a supplier cannot meet a standard clause?
items.scenario: Before onboarding a managed payroll provider, an organisation mapped the data processed, required encryption and breach notification within 24 hours, and added a right to receive annual assurance reports. When the provider later changed a sub-processor, the contractual approval clause triggered a review that identified missing transfer safeguards before processing began.

items.title: Managing information security in the ICT supply chain
items.objective: Manages information security risks associated with the ICT supply chain, including components, services and dependencies provided by suppliers and their subcontractors.
items.whyItExists: ICT products and services often include hidden dependencies, outsourced development, cloud components and fourth parties. Weaknesses anywhere in that chain can affect confidentiality, integrity and availability, so security management must extend beyond the direct supplier relationship.
items.riskAddressed: Compromise or failure introduced through upstream ICT components, service dependencies or subcontractors that are not visible or governed.
items.implementationGuidance: Identify critical ICT suppliers and the components or services they provide, including software, hardware, cloud platforms and managed services. Require transparency on provenance, secure development practices, vulnerability handling, support lifetimes and subcontracting where relevant. Assess supply-chain risks during selection and periodically thereafter, monitor advisories and end-of-support notices, and maintain contingency plans for supplier failure or compromise. Ensure contracts and onboarding capture obligations for downstream parties and that changes in the supply chain trigger reassessment.
evidenceExamples: ICT supplier inventory with criticality and dependency mapping
Supplier security and provenance assessments
Advisory and vulnerability monitoring records
Contingency plans for critical ICT dependencies
items.auditTesting: Review critical ICT services and confirm supply-chain risks were identified, assessed and monitored. Test whether subcontractor changes, vulnerability disclosures or end-of-support events resulted in documented decisions and actions.
commonGaps: No inventory of critical ICT dependencies or fourth parties
Reliance on supplier reputation without evidence
End-of-support components not tracked
No contingency plan for critical service compromise
interviewQuestions: Which ICT suppliers are critical to your operations and why?
How do you learn about vulnerabilities or subcontractor changes in the supply chain?
What is your fallback if a critical cloud or software supplier fails?
items.scenario: A financial services firm mapped dependencies for its customer portal and discovered a niche authentication component maintained by a subcontractor. By requiring disclosure and monitoring support status, the firm planned migration before the component reached end of support and avoided an unsupported security exposure.

items.title: Monitoring, review and change management of supplier services
items.objective: Ensures supplier services are monitored, reviewed and reassessed over time, including when service changes, incidents or risk conditions affect security.
items.whyItExists: Supplier risk is not static: services evolve, personnel and subcontractors change, incidents occur and assurance reports expire. Ongoing monitoring confirms that agreed controls continue to operate and that changes do not introduce unmanaged risk.
items.riskAddressed: Degraded or changed supplier controls that go unnoticed after onboarding, leading to service disruption, data exposure or loss of assurance.
items.implementationGuidance: Define monitoring activities proportionate to supplier tier, such as service reviews, KPI and SLA tracking, security report review, incident follow-up, reassessment cycles and change notifications. Require suppliers to communicate material changes to services, locations, subcontractors or security posture. Record review outcomes, track remediation actions to closure, and escalate significant issues through governance forums. Reassess suppliers at contract renewal, after incidents or when business dependence increases.
items.responsibleDepartment: Third Party Risk / Service Owners / Information Security
evidenceExamples: Supplier review meeting minutes and KPI reports
Periodic reassessment records
Supplier change notifications and impact assessments
Remediation tracker with closure evidence
items.auditTesting: Sample active suppliers and verify monitoring occurred according to tier, issues were tracked and material changes or incidents triggered reassessment or escalation. Confirm evidence is retained and current.
commonGaps: Onboarding assessment performed but no ongoing reviews
Supplier changes accepted without security impact assessment
Remediation actions tracked informally
Expired assurance reports not refreshed
interviewQuestions: How often do you review this supplier’s security performance?
What triggers an out-of-cycle reassessment?
Show evidence that a supplier issue was tracked to closure.
items.scenario: A cloud service provider notified a customer of a new data processing location. Because change monitoring was defined, the service owner assessed legal and security impact, updated records and obtained confirmation of equivalent controls before the change took effect.

items.title: Information security for use of cloud services
items.objective: Establishes processes for acquiring, using, managing and exiting cloud services securely in line with information security requirements.
items.whyItExists: Cloud services introduce shared responsibility, internet exposure, rapid configuration change and dependence on provider controls. Clear governance is needed to select appropriate services, configure them securely, monitor use and plan exit so that data and operations remain protected.
items.riskAddressed: Misconfigured or poorly governed cloud services leading to data exposure, unauthorised access, compliance gaps or inability to recover or exit.
items.implementationGuidance: Define cloud adoption and approval processes that assess data classification, regulatory needs, shared responsibility, identity integration, logging, encryption, resilience and exit options before use. Maintain an inventory of approved cloud services, apply secure configuration baselines, restrict administrative access, monitor for misconfiguration and anomalous activity, and review provider assurance. Document responsibilities between the organisation and provider, and ensure contracts and procedures support data portability, backup and secure deletion at termination.
items.responsibleDepartment: Cloud Governance / Information Security / IT Operations
evidenceExamples: Approved cloud service inventory
Cloud risk assessments and shared responsibility mappings
Configuration baseline and monitoring evidence
Exit and data portability plans for critical services
items.auditTesting: Review selected cloud services and confirm approval, risk assessment, secure configuration and monitoring are in place. Verify responsibilities are understood and exit or continuity considerations are documented for critical services.
commonGaps: Shadow cloud services adopted without assessment
Shared responsibility misunderstood
No monitoring for misconfiguration or excessive permissions
No exit or data return plan
interviewQuestions: How do you approve a new cloud service before business use?
Who is responsible for configuring security controls in this service?
How would you retrieve and delete data if the service were terminated?
items.scenario: A team adopted a collaboration platform for project files without security review. After introducing a cloud approval workflow, the organisation classified data, enabled MFA and logging, restricted external sharing and recorded an exit plan, reducing exposure from unmanaged configuration.

items.title: Information security incident management planning and preparation
items.objective: Defines and maintains the organisation’s incident management structure, responsibilities, procedures and readiness activities so incidents can be handled consistently and effectively.
items.whyItExists: Security incidents require rapid, coordinated decisions under pressure. Without prior planning, roles, escalation paths, evidence handling and communication channels are unclear, increasing impact, recovery time and the risk of regulatory or legal missteps.
items.riskAddressed: Delayed, inconsistent or ineffective incident response due to lack of preparation, unclear authority or missing procedures.
items.implementationGuidance: Establish an incident management policy and plan covering detection sources, triage criteria, severity levels, roles, escalation, communication, evidence preservation, containment, recovery and post-incident review. Maintain contact lists, playbooks for likely scenarios, tooling access and decision authorities. Train responders, run exercises, and coordinate with legal, privacy, communications, business continuity and supplier contacts where relevant. Review and update plans after exercises, incidents and organisational changes.
evidenceExamples: Incident response plan and playbooks
Roles, escalation matrix and contact lists
Exercise reports and training records
Tooling and evidence handling procedures
items.auditTesting: Inspect incident management documentation and confirm it is current, approved and practical. Verify responders are trained, exercises are performed and lessons learned lead to updates in plans or controls.
commonGaps: Plan exists but is outdated or untested
Escalation contacts and authorities unclear
No playbooks for common incident types
Exercises conducted without tracked improvements
interviewQuestions: Who has authority to declare a major incident and escalate externally?
When was the incident response plan last exercised?
How are lessons learned incorporated into preparation?
items.scenario: An organisation ran a ransomware tabletop exercise and found legal notification steps were unclear and backup contacts were outdated. Updating the plan, contacts and playbooks before a real event reduced confusion and improved decision speed during a later malware incident.

items.title: Assessment and decision on information security events
items.objective: Ensures information security events are assessed promptly to determine whether they constitute incidents and what response priority or action is required.
items.whyItExists: Not every event is an incident, but missed or misclassified events can allow real incidents to escalate. A consistent assessment process supports timely escalation, appropriate prioritisation and accurate records.
items.riskAddressed: Security events overlooked, misclassified or escalated too late, increasing potential damage and reducing response effectiveness.
items.implementationGuidance: Define criteria for identifying, categorising and prioritising events based on impact, scope, affected assets, data sensitivity and threat indicators. Provide intake channels and logging for reported events, assign qualified personnel to triage, and record assessment decisions and rationale. Establish time expectations for initial assessment and escalation, integrate automated alerts where appropriate, and ensure handover to incident response when thresholds are met.
evidenceExamples: Event reporting and triage procedures
Event and incident logs with classification decisions
Alerting and escalation criteria
Triage training or competency records
items.auditTesting: Sample reported events and alerts to confirm they were logged, assessed against defined criteria and escalated or closed with documented rationale within expected timeframes.
commonGaps: No consistent severity or classification criteria
Events handled informally without records
Alerts not reviewed or correlated
Escalation thresholds unclear
interviewQuestions: How do you decide whether an event becomes an incident?
Show a recent example of triage and the rationale for the decision.
What is the expected time to assess a high-priority alert?
items.scenario: A service desk received reports of unusual login prompts. Using defined triage criteria, analysts correlated alerts, identified credential phishing as a likely incident and escalated within minutes, enabling account resets before further compromise.

items.title: Response to information security incidents
items.objective: Requires information security incidents to be responded to according to documented procedures to contain impact, eradicate causes and recover services.
items.whyItExists: Effective response limits damage, preserves evidence and restores normal operations. Ad hoc actions can worsen outages, destroy forensic value or leave attackers with continued access.
items.riskAddressed: Uncoordinated or incomplete incident response causing extended disruption, recurring compromise or loss of evidence needed for investigation and reporting.
items.implementationGuidance: Execute incident response procedures based on incident type and severity, including containment, evidence preservation, eradication, recovery and communication. Assign an incident lead, coordinate technical and business stakeholders, document actions and decisions, and manage external parties such as providers, regulators or law enforcement when required. Confirm systems are safe before restoration, monitor for recurrence and capture indicators to improve detection and controls.
evidenceExamples: Incident records with timeline and actions taken
Containment and recovery evidence
Communication and notification records
Forensic or evidence handling logs where applicable
items.auditTesting: Review incident records and confirm response followed approved procedures, actions were documented, containment and recovery were effective and required communications occurred. Check for evidence of post-recovery monitoring.
commonGaps: Response actions not documented
Systems restored without confirming eradication
Evidence overwritten during recovery
Required stakeholders not engaged
interviewQuestions: Walk me through the response to a recent incident.
How do you preserve evidence while restoring service?
Who approves returning affected systems to production?
items.scenario: During a malware outbreak, responders isolated affected endpoints, preserved disk images, removed persistence mechanisms and restored from clean backups. Documented actions supported internal reporting and helped identify a missing patching control.

items.title: Learning from information security incidents
items.objective: Ensures information from security incidents is analysed to identify root causes, improve controls and reduce the likelihood or impact of recurrence.
items.whyItExists: Incidents reveal weaknesses in prevention, detection and response. Without structured learning, organisations repeat the same failures and miss opportunities to strengthen resilience and awareness.
items.riskAddressed: Recurring incidents and persistent control gaps because lessons are not identified, prioritised or implemented.
items.implementationGuidance: Conduct post-incident reviews for relevant incidents to analyse root causes, contributing factors, response effectiveness and business impact. Record lessons learned, assign corrective and preventive actions with owners and due dates, and track them to completion. Share appropriate findings with affected teams, update risk assessments, playbooks, training and controls, and report trends to management for oversight.
evidenceExamples: Post-incident review reports
Corrective action plans and closure evidence
Updated playbooks, risks or control records
Management trend reports
items.auditTesting: Sample incidents and verify reviews were performed where appropriate, root causes considered, actions assigned and completed, and improvements reflected in documentation, controls or training.
commonGaps: No post-incident reviews for significant incidents
Actions identified but not tracked
Lessons not shared beyond the technical team
Recurring incidents with unchanged controls
interviewQuestions: How do you decide which incidents require a formal review?
Show an improvement implemented as a result of an incident.
How are incident trends reported to management?
items.scenario: After repeated phishing-related account compromises, reviews identified weak MFA coverage for legacy applications. The organisation prioritised MFA expansion and targeted awareness, reducing similar incidents in subsequent quarters.

items.title: Collection of evidence
items.objective: Establishes procedures for identifying, collecting, preserving and handling evidence related to information security events in a manner suitable for analysis and potential legal or disciplinary use.
items.whyItExists: Poor evidence handling can undermine investigations, prevent accurate determination of cause and make findings unusable in disciplinary, contractual or legal proceedings. Preserving integrity and chain of custody is essential when incidents may have formal consequences.
items.riskAddressed: Loss, contamination or inadmissibility of evidence needed to investigate incidents, support decisions or meet legal obligations.
items.implementationGuidance: Define evidence handling procedures covering identification, collection, labelling, storage, access, transfer and retention. Maintain chain-of-custody records, use appropriate tools and methods to preserve integrity, and restrict access to authorised personnel. Coordinate with legal, HR and law enforcement requirements where applicable, and train responders on when and how to collect evidence without unnecessarily disrupting operations.
evidenceExamples: Evidence handling procedures
Chain-of-custody forms and evidence logs
Secure evidence storage records
Responder training materials
items.auditTesting: Review procedures and sampled investigations to confirm evidence was identified, preserved and documented appropriately. Verify chain of custody, access controls and retention align with policy and legal needs.
commonGaps: Evidence collected without documentation
Uncontrolled access to forensic images or logs
Logs overwritten before preservation
No guidance for legal or disciplinary cases
interviewQuestions: How do you maintain chain of custody during an investigation?
Where is evidence stored and who can access it?
When do you involve legal in evidence collection?
items.scenario: When suspicious data exfiltration was detected, responders captured relevant logs and system images, recorded hashes and maintained a chain-of-custody log. The preserved evidence supported a confirmed timeline and informed HR and contractual actions.

items.title: Information security during disruption
items.objective: Ensures information security is planned, maintained and adapted during disruptions so that critical information and services remain appropriately protected.
items.whyItExists: Disruptions such as outages, disasters or supplier failures can pressure teams to bypass controls to restore service. Planning helps maintain essential security protections and avoid creating additional incidents during crisis response.
items.riskAddressed: Security controls weakened or bypassed during disruption, leading to data loss, unauthorised access or prolonged recovery.
items.implementationGuidance: Integrate information security requirements into business continuity and disaster recovery planning, including minimum security controls during degraded operations, access restrictions, backup integrity, secure recovery procedures and communication safeguards. Identify critical assets and dependencies, define acceptable temporary measures with approval, and test continuity arrangements. Coordinate with incident response and suppliers to ensure security considerations are addressed throughout disruption and restoration.
evidenceExamples: Business continuity and disaster recovery plans with security requirements
Disruption risk assessments
Test or exercise results
Records of approved temporary control deviations
items.auditTesting: Review continuity plans and exercise results to confirm security requirements are included and tested. Verify temporary measures during disruptions are risk-assessed, approved and reversed when normal operations resume.
commonGaps: Continuity plans focus on availability but ignore confidentiality and integrity
Emergency access not controlled or reviewed
Backups not protected or tested for secure recovery
Temporary workarounds become permanent
interviewQuestions: How are security controls maintained during a major outage?
What temporary measures are allowed in an emergency and who approves them?
When were continuity plans last tested with security in scope?
items.scenario: During a data centre outage, a company activated a recovery site with predefined access controls, encrypted backup restoration and documented emergency access. Temporary firewall exceptions were approved, time-limited and removed after service stabilisation.

items.title: ICT readiness for business continuity
items.objective: Ensures ICT services and supporting infrastructure are prepared to meet availability and recovery requirements during disruption.
items.whyItExists: Business continuity depends on ICT systems, networks, data and suppliers being recoverable within required timeframes. Readiness planning, redundancy and testing reduce downtime and support orderly recovery.
items.riskAddressed: Inability to restore critical ICT services within required objectives, causing operational, financial or regulatory impact.
items.implementationGuidance: Identify critical ICT services and define recovery objectives such as RTO and RPO with business owners. Implement resilience measures including backups, redundancy, failover, capacity planning and dependency management. Document recovery procedures, maintain current configurations and contact information, and test restoration and failover regularly. Address cloud and supplier dependencies, and update plans after changes, tests or incidents.
evidenceExamples: ICT continuity and recovery plans
RTO/RPO definitions for critical services
Backup, failover and restoration test records
Dependency and capacity planning documentation
items.auditTesting: Review critical services and confirm recovery objectives are defined, supported by technical measures and tested. Verify test results, issues and improvements are documented and plans reflect current architecture.
commonGaps: Recovery objectives undefined or unrealistic
Backups untested or incomplete
Dependencies on suppliers or components not considered
Plans outdated after system changes
interviewQuestions: What are the RTO and RPO for this critical system?
When was the last successful restoration test?
Which dependencies could prevent recovery?
items.scenario: A company identified its order processing system as critical and implemented replicated databases and documented failover steps. Quarterly tests revealed a missing configuration backup, which was added to the recovery procedure before any real outage occurred.

items.title: Legal, statutory, regulatory and contractual requirements
items.objective: Identifies, documents and keeps up to date legal, statutory, regulatory and contractual requirements relevant to information security and the organisation’s approach to meeting them.
items.whyItExists: Information security obligations arise from laws, regulations, contracts and industry requirements. If they are not identified and tracked, the organisation may unknowingly violate obligations, miss reporting duties or fail to implement required controls.
items.riskAddressed: Non-compliance with applicable legal, regulatory or contractual information security requirements.
items.implementationGuidance: Maintain a register of applicable requirements covering privacy, security, records, sector regulation, contractual clauses and cross-border obligations. Assign owners, map requirements to controls and processes, monitor changes, and review applicability when services, locations or data types change. Communicate obligations to relevant teams, integrate them into policies and procedures, and retain evidence of compliance activities and decisions.
evidenceExamples: Compliance obligations register
Requirement-to-control mapping
Change monitoring and review records
Evidence of compliance assessments
items.auditTesting: Review the obligations register for completeness, currency and ownership. Sample requirements and verify they are mapped to controls, communicated and supported by evidence of compliance or tracked remediation.
commonGaps: Register incomplete or outdated
No owner for specific obligations
Requirements identified but not implemented
Contractual security clauses overlooked
interviewQuestions: How do you identify new legal or regulatory security requirements?
Show how a specific requirement maps to controls and evidence.
Who owns compliance for contractual security obligations?
items.scenario: A company expanding into a new region reviewed privacy and breach notification laws before launch, updated contracts and incident procedures, and assigned local compliance owners, avoiding missed notification duties.

items.title: Intellectual property rights
items.objective: Ensures appropriate procedures are implemented to protect intellectual property rights associated with software, documents, data and other information assets.
items.whyItExists: Unauthorised use, copying or distribution of intellectual property can create legal liability, financial penalties and reputational harm. Organisations must also protect their own intellectual property from misuse or leakage.
items.riskAddressed: Legal breaches, licence violations or loss of proprietary information due to inadequate protection of intellectual property rights.
items.implementationGuidance: Maintain inventories of licensed software, media and third-party content, and ensure use complies with licence terms. Implement procedures for acquiring, tracking and retiring licences, prevent installation of unauthorised software, and protect proprietary information through classification, access controls and contractual terms. Educate users on acceptable use and report suspected infringement promptly for legal review.
items.responsibleDepartment: Legal / IT Asset Management / Information Security
evidenceExamples: Software and licence inventory
Acceptable use and IP procedures
Records of licence procurement and compliance checks
Contracts protecting proprietary information
items.auditTesting: Verify licence records are maintained and reconciled to installed or used software where applicable. Sample proprietary assets and confirm access, handling and contractual protections align with policy.
commonGaps: Unlicensed or untracked software use
No process for validating licence terms
Proprietary information shared without protection
Users unaware of IP obligations
interviewQuestions: How do you track software licences and compliance?
What controls protect proprietary designs or source code?
How are suspected infringement issues handled?
items.scenario: An internal review found several teams using unlicensed design tools. By centralising procurement, maintaining a licence inventory and restricting unauthorised installs, the organisation reduced legal exposure and improved cost control.

items.title: Protection of records
items.objective: Protects records from loss, destruction, falsification, unauthorised access and unauthorised release in accordance with legal, regulatory, contractual and business requirements.
items.whyItExists: Records provide evidence of business activities, decisions and compliance. If records are not protected and retained appropriately, the organisation may be unable to meet legal obligations, support investigations or demonstrate control operation.
items.riskAddressed: Loss, alteration or inappropriate disclosure of records required for business, legal or compliance purposes.
items.implementationGuidance: Identify record types and define retention, storage, protection, access, retrieval and disposal requirements based on business value and obligations. Implement controls such as access restrictions, backups, integrity protections, audit trails and secure disposal. Ensure records stored in physical and electronic systems, including cloud services, are covered by procedures and periodically reviewed for compliance with retention schedules.
evidenceExamples: Records retention schedule
Storage and access control procedures
Backup and integrity evidence for key records
Disposal and destruction records
items.auditTesting: Sample records across systems and confirm retention, protection, access and disposal align with defined requirements. Verify integrity and availability controls operate for records needed for compliance or business continuity.
commonGaps: No retention schedule or inconsistent application
Records stored in unmanaged locations
Excessive access to sensitive records
Records retained longer than necessary without justification
interviewQuestions: How do you determine how long different records must be kept?
What protects records from unauthorised alteration?
How are records securely disposed of at end of retention?
items.scenario: A compliance team could not produce complete audit evidence because logs and approvals were stored in personal mailboxes. Implementing a records schedule and controlled repositories improved retrieval and evidential integrity.

items.title: Privacy and protection of PII
items.objective: Ensures privacy and protection of personally identifiable information (PII) as required by applicable laws, regulations and contractual obligations.
items.whyItExists: Processing PII creates obligations to individuals and regulators. Failure to protect privacy can cause harm to individuals, legal penalties, loss of trust and restrictions on business activities.
items.riskAddressed: Unlawful, unfair or insecure processing of PII resulting in privacy harm, regulatory action or reputational damage.
items.implementationGuidance: Identify PII processed by the organisation, define lawful purposes and handling requirements, and implement policies and controls for collection, use, storage, sharing, retention and deletion. Apply minimisation, access restrictions, encryption where appropriate, transparency and rights-handling processes. Assess privacy risks for new or changed processing, manage processor obligations, and respond to incidents involving PII according to legal and contractual requirements.
evidenceExamples: PII inventory or records of processing
Privacy policies and notices
Data processing agreements and assessments
PII incident and rights request records
items.auditTesting: Review PII processing activities and confirm purposes, controls and retention are defined and implemented. Sample systems or vendors processing PII and verify contractual, technical and procedural protections are in place.
commonGaps: PII processing not fully identified
Excessive collection or retention
Weak controls for sharing with processors
No clear process for privacy incidents or rights requests
interviewQuestions: What PII do you process and for what purposes?
How do you ensure vendors protect PII appropriately?
How are retention and deletion requirements enforced?
items.scenario: A marketing team collected customer data for multiple campaigns without clear retention limits. A privacy review defined purposes, minimised fields, updated notices and implemented deletion schedules aligned to policy.

items.title: Independent review of information security
items.objective: Ensures the organisation’s approach to managing information security, including policies, processes and controls, is independently reviewed at planned intervals or when significant changes occur.
items.whyItExists: Independent review provides objective assurance on whether security arrangements are appropriate, implemented and effective. Without it, weaknesses may persist unnoticed or be assessed with bias by those responsible for operating controls.
items.riskAddressed: Undetected weaknesses in information security governance, controls or compliance due to lack of objective review.
items.implementationGuidance: Plan independent reviews based on risk, regulatory expectations and significant changes such as new systems, major incidents or reorganisations. Use qualified internal or external reviewers independent of the activities being assessed, define scope and criteria, and report findings to management. Track remediation actions, verify closure and consider review results in risk assessments and improvement planning.
evidenceExamples: Independent review plan and reports
Reviewer independence and competence evidence
Management responses and remediation tracker
Follow-up verification records
items.auditTesting: Verify reviews are performed by independent parties at planned intervals or after significant changes. Sample findings and confirm management actions were assigned, implemented and verified.
commonGaps: Reviews performed by control owners without independence
No follow-up on findings
Scope too narrow to assess key risks
Reviews infrequent despite major changes
interviewQuestions: Who performs independent security reviews and how is independence ensured?
How are review findings tracked to closure?
When was the last review triggered by a significant change?
items.scenario: After migrating core services to cloud, an organisation commissioned an independent assessment of identity, logging and supplier controls. Findings were prioritised in the risk register and verified in a follow-up review.

items.title: Compliance with policies, rules and standards for information security
items.objective: Ensures compliance with the organisation’s information security policies, rules and standards is regularly reviewed and deviations are addressed.
items.whyItExists: Policies and standards only reduce risk when they are followed. Regular compliance checks identify gaps, misunderstandings and exceptions so they can be corrected before causing incidents or audit findings.
items.riskAddressed: Persistent non-compliance with internal security requirements leading to control failures and unmanaged risk.
items.implementationGuidance: Define compliance review methods such as self-assessments, automated checks, configuration reviews, audits and metrics. Assign responsibilities for monitoring, report results to relevant managers, and require corrective actions for deviations with defined timelines. Manage exceptions formally with approval, compensating controls and review dates. Use results to improve awareness, tooling and policy clarity.
evidenceExamples: Compliance review reports and checklists
Automated policy or configuration compliance results
Exception register and approvals
Corrective action tracking
items.auditTesting: Sample policies or standards and verify compliance is monitored through defined methods. Confirm deviations are recorded, remediated or formally approved as exceptions with review.
commonGaps: Compliance assumed but not measured
Exceptions undocumented or never reviewed
Findings reported without corrective action
No ownership for monitoring specific standards
interviewQuestions: How do you measure compliance with key security policies?
Show an example of a deviation and how it was resolved.
How are exceptions approved and reviewed?
items.scenario: A quarterly configuration review showed several systems missing required logging settings. Owners remediated configurations, updated deployment templates and recorded a short-term exception for one legacy system with compensating monitoring.

items.title: Documented operating procedures
items.objective: Ensures operating procedures for information processing facilities are documented and made available to personnel who need them.
items.whyItExists: Consistent, documented procedures reduce errors, support secure operation and enable continuity when staff change or incidents occur. Undocumented processes rely on individual knowledge and increase operational and security risk.
items.riskAddressed: Operational errors, inconsistent control execution or delayed recovery due to missing or unclear procedures.
items.implementationGuidance: Identify activities requiring documented procedures, such as system administration, backup, change handling, access management, monitoring and incident response support tasks. Document steps, responsibilities, prerequisites, security controls and escalation paths in clear language. Store procedures in accessible controlled locations, review them periodically and update them after system or process changes. Train relevant personnel and restrict editing to authorised owners.
evidenceExamples: Documented operating procedures repository
Procedure review and version history
Training or acknowledgement records
Change records triggering procedure updates
items.auditTesting: Sample critical operational activities and confirm procedures exist, are current, accessible to relevant staff and reflect actual practice. Verify updates occur after relevant changes or incidents.
commonGaps: Procedures outdated or stored informally
Critical tasks dependent on individual knowledge
No version control or review cycle
Procedures not followed in practice
interviewQuestions: Where are operating procedures maintained and how are they kept current?
Show the procedure for a critical operational task.
How do staff know when a procedure changes?
items.scenario: After a backup failure during restoration, a team discovered the recovery steps were incomplete and known only to one administrator. Documenting and testing the procedure improved recovery consistency and reduced dependency on individuals.
